summary: The instructions address unintentional violations and prescribe a sin offering according to who is responsible: the anointed priest, the whole congregation, a ruler, or one of the common people. Blood for the priest and congregation enters the Tent, while blood for a ruler or common person is applied to the outer altar. The congregation, ruler, and common-person cases explicitly end in atonement and forgiveness; the priest’s opening case does not repeat that formula.
whyItMatters: This chapter makes accountability extend across every level of the community while carefully distinguishing how each case affects the sanctuary and is addressed there.

context.author: The chapter presents Yahweh speaking these instructions to Moses; it does not identify the book's narrator or final compiler.
context.audience: The children of Israel, including priests, the assembled congregation, rulers, and individual members of the people.
context.date: The narrative setting is Israel's time at Sinai; the chapter itself does not date its composition.
context.setting: At the Tent of Meeting, with actions performed both inside the sanctuary area and outside the camp.
context.literaryForm: Priestly case instruction arranged by the standing of the person or group responsible for an unintentional violation.

outline.heading: The anointed priest's sin offering
outline.note: A bull's blood is brought into the Tent, and the rest of the animal is burned outside the camp.

outline.heading: The congregation's sin offering
outline.note: The elders identify with a bull, and the priest follows the sanctuary procedure used in the first case.

outline.heading: A ruler's sin offering
outline.note: A male goat is brought, and its blood is applied to the altar of burnt offering rather than carried inside.

outline.heading: A common person's goat
outline.note: An individual may bring a female goat, after which the priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven.

outline.heading: A common person's lamb
outline.note: A female lamb provides a second case with the same closing assurance of atonement and forgiveness.

keyVerses.text: “Speak to the children of Israel, saying, ‘If anyone sins unintentionally, in any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, and does any one of them,
keyVerses.why: The opening limits the chapter's cases to violations committed unintentionally.

keyVerses.text: when the sin in which they have sinned is known, then the assembly shall offer a young bull for a sin offering, and bring it before the Tent of Meeting.
keyVerses.why: Once a hidden communal violation becomes known, the assembly must bring a bull for a sin offering.

keyVerses.text: He shall do this with the bull; as he did with the bull of the sin offering, so he shall do with this; and the priest shall make atonement for them, and they shall be forgiven.
keyVerses.why: The congregation’s case reaches the chapter’s repeated destination: priestly atonement followed by forgiveness.

keyVerses.text: “‘If anyone of the common people sins unwittingly, in doing any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, and is guilty,
keyVerses.why: The final major case makes clear that the same issue reaches ordinary members of the community, not only leaders.

themes: blood applied to sanctuary and altar

questions.question: What is a sin offering in this chapter?
questions.answer: It is the prescribed offering when a prohibited act was committed unintentionally. Animal and blood procedures vary by the responsible party; the congregation, ruler, and common-person cases explicitly end with priestly atonement and forgiveness, while the priest’s first case does not state that closing result.

questions.question: Why does an unintentional act still create guilt?
questions.answer: That is the chapter's starting assumption: lack of intent does not erase the violation once it becomes known. The text provides a path for addressing it, but it does not equate an accident with deliberate wrongdoing or discuss their relative severity here.

questions.question: How can the anointed priest's sin bring guilt on the people?
questions.answer: Verse 3 explicitly treats the anointed priest’s failure as bringing guilt on the people and requires a bull whose blood is taken into the Tent. The congregation receives a comparable procedure, and the chapter does not describe the exact chain of responsibility, so a specific incident or mechanism should not be invented.

questions.question: How can the whole congregation sin without noticing?
questions.answer: The text says the matter can be hidden from the assembly's eyes and later become known. It does not supply an example, but it treats a community as capable of shared action and shared guilt even when recognition comes after the act.

questions.question: Why is blood taken inside for the priest and congregation but not for the other cases?
questions.answer: For the priest and congregation, blood is sprinkled before the veil and placed on the incense altar; for a ruler or common person, it is placed on the burnt-offering altar. The chapter consistently distinguishes the procedures but does not explain the reason for that distinction.

questions.question: Why is most of the bull burned outside the camp?
questions.answer: Both the priest's bull and the congregation's bull are taken to the clean ash place outside the camp and burned there after their blood and fat are handled. The chapter gives that location as part of the rite without explaining a symbolic or sanitary reason.

questions.question: What does the repeated promise of forgiveness contribute?
questions.answer: The ruler, common-person goat, and common-person lamb cases each close by saying the priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven; the congregation receives the same assurance. The repetition makes restoration, not permanent exclusion, the endpoint of these procedures.

questions.question: Do the different animals imply that some people matter more to God?
questions.answer: The chapter varies animals and blood procedures according to whether the responsible party is priest, congregation, ruler, or common person. It explicitly gives the same forgiveness outcome to the last three cases and makes no statement that the differing sacrifices assign greater human worth; the priest’s first case simply lacks a closing forgiveness formula.

glossary.def: The sacrifice prescribed here for an unintentional prohibited act that has become known.
The priest set apart for office with anointing, whose failure is treated in the chapter's first case.
Israel considered as an assembled community, represented in this procedure by its elders.
Projections at the altar's corners on which the priest places blood in these rites.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The peace-offering rules close by reserving fat for the altar and prohibiting consumption of blood.

here.text: Unintentional violations are treated in separate cases for the anointed priest, the congregation, a ruler, and an individual. Blood enters the Tent in the first two cases but goes on the outer altar in the latter cases.

after.text: The next chapter names concrete liabilities such as withheld testimony, unrecognized ritual contact, and rash oaths, then allows less costly offerings and addresses trespass against holy things.
